title: Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS)
objectives: The two main objectives for BASS are to: 1.) Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test#1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity. The relation between these can be investigated by observing flames burning for the longer times available in flight. Practical, realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including wake flames which have characteristics of a fire burning behind another object (for example, a fire burning in tight area which may not be easily accessible). 2.) Assess the effectiveness of an inert, gaseous extinguishing agent (similar to that used on ISS) in putting out flames over different materials, geometries, preheating, and flow.
approach: The experiment was conducted aboard the International Space Station (ISS) inside the Microgravity Glove Box (MSG). Custom-made fabric samples consisting of 75% cotton and 25% fiberglass (by mass) were used as a fuel source as well as Nomex fabric and Ultem. A Kanthal wire (29-gage) igniter was used to initiate combustion at one end of the fabric. Airflow was controlled using a variable speed fan, with airflow speeds reaching as high as 40 cm/s. The airflow was directed along the fuel surface in either the opposed or concurrent direction. This investigation explored two primary air flow configurations; concurrent-flow and opposed-flow. With concurrent-flow air flows in the same direction as the flame spread and in opposed-flow air flows in the opposite direction of flame spread. Flames were observed in the top and edge profiles and data was collected on flame size, shape, color, spread rate, and potential flame quenching. The samples were placed in a small flow duct (76 mm x 76 mm cross section) that allowed for airflow across the fabric. Other sample shapes were utilized as well including spheres and cylinders.
hypothesis: BASS experiments were based on the hypothesis that materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well if not better than the same material in normal gravity with other conditions being identical (pressure, oxygen concentration, temperature, etc.) To test this hypothesis with any but the thinnest materials requires extended microgravity time – longer than available in drop towers or parabolic aircraft.
impacts: Current NASA spacecraft materials selection is based on a standard test method (NASA–STD–6001 Test 1) that segregates material based on 1-g behavior without consideration of low gravity effects. A critical element of this understanding is the radiative heat emission from the flame. These results are used in first order models and predictions of heat release in spacecraft fires and as a means to extend heat release data from tests like the NASA cone calorimeter test (NASA–STD–6001 Test 2) to a performance-based material selection process. Using nitrogen as a flame suppressant in microgravity provides a direct link to current and planned extinguishment techniques. BASS results provide essential guidance to ground-based microgravity combustion research efforts. Detailed combustion models are validated using the simpler flow environment afforded by tests in microgravity. Once validated, they can be used to build more complex combustion models needed to capture the important details of flames burning in normal gravity. These models have wide applicability to the general understanding of many terrestrial combustion problems and will guide novel spacecraft design and ensure the safety of future crewed missions.

title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II (BASS-II)

key_conditions.oxygen: varied below 21% by nitrogen vitiation (e.g. 22.2% initial in sample rows)

objectives: BASS-II results contribute to the combustion computational models used in the design of fire detection and suppression systems in microgravity and on Earth. Objectives Include: 1) Study the ignition, flame growth, flame spread, and extinction limits for solid fuels burning in low-velocity forced flows in microgravity. 2) Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test #1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity. 3) Provide SoFIE PIs with preliminary data to refine Science Requirements. 4) Practical, realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including slabs, cylinders, and spherical sections. The primary variables include: Forced flow velocity (speed and direction); Ambient oxygen concentration (via working volume nitrogen vitiation); Sample geometry (rods, spherical section, slabs, films, and fabric sheets).
approach: Microgravity combustion tests were performed aboard the International Space Station. Active crew support for real-time 'lab partner' operations. The wind tunnel was installed in the Microgravity Science Glovebox which supplied power, imaging, and a level of containment. Fuel samples were mounted inside a small wind tunnel which could impose airflow speeds up to 40 cm/s. Main variables are airflow speed and oxygen concentration (oxygen varied below 21% by adding nitrogen). Flame appearance, flame growth, and spread rates were determined in both the opposed and concurrent flow.
hypothesis: BASS–II tests the hypothesis that materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well if not better than the same material in normal gravity with other conditions being identical (pressure, O2 concentration, temperature, etc.). NASA tests and controls materials from a flammability perspective using an upward burning test in normal gravity, which is considered to be the worst-case geometry for flammability of the material on Earth. However, it may not be conservative for flammability in space. Testing at constant O2 mole fractions permits studying flame spread and extinction at low and high flow speed. We are interested in finding the fundamental limit for a given material.
impacts: A primary goal of BASS-II is improved spacecraft fire safety, improved understanding of combustion in space and how to avoid it. If you're on a mission far from Earth, a fire can be catastrophic. BASS-II helps engineers select the safest materials and improve firefighting methods on future space missions. In outer space, fuels burn as oval balls rather than with an upward pointed cone flame as they do on Earth. This simpler combustion process enables researchers to evaluate computer models of fuel burning. These models can then be used to more accurately study flames on Earth, such as in wildfires, building fires, energy recapture from waste recycling, and other combustion problems.

Subrata Bhattacharjee (Co-I, San Diego State University)

title: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I (SAFFIRE-I)
platform: Cygnus resupply vehicle after deberthing from ISS (PSI page lists ISS)
fuels: SIBAL fabric (75% cotton / 25% fiberglass), 94 cm x 40.6 cm, 0.37 cm thick
objectives: The objectives of this investigation were to: (1) determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity and (2) investigate the low-g flammability limits compared to those obtained in NASA's normal gravity material flammability screening test.
approach: The Saffire-1 experiment was performed on the Orbital Science's Cygnus resupply vehicle after it deberthed from the ISS. The sample material for Saffire-I is a composite fabric called Sibal consisting of cotton on a fiberglass substrate (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass by weight). It has been used in many space experiments because it burns like cotton but maintains structural integrity after the cotton is consumed. The sample was approximately 0.94 meters long and 0.4 meters wide, simulating a large piece of flammable fabric. The Saffire-1 flight unit had a sample card installed in the middle of a large flow duct. Air is drawn through the flow duct by fans located at the top of the duct with flow straighteners at the bottom of the experiment module. Saffire-I was conducted at an air flow velocity of 20 cm/s. Once the sample was ignited flame images were captured using two cameras. In addition, thermocouples provided flow, flame, and plume temperatures, two radiometers recorded flame radiation, solid state sensors were used to measure pressure, CO2 and O2 mole fraction, and two anemometers tracked flow velocity. All data was compressed, and subsequently downlinked.
hypothesis: This investigation hypothesizes that due to large differences between fire behavior in normal and reduced gravity, the use of terrestrial fires and fire standards to design spacecraft fire safety systems presents an inherent risk to the vehicle because of the significant level of uncertainty. While this approach has been successful thus far, the uncertainty and risk will increase as exploration missions venture further from earth with considerably longer transit times for a safe return. There is a significant lack of microgravity data available for spacecraft designers on which to base their fire safety designs and procedures. To address this knowledge gap, this investigation proposed to conduct large-scale fire safety experiments in an expendable spacecraft without risk to a crew.
impacts: The Saffire-I experiment provides a new way to study a realistic fire on an exploration vehicle, which has not been possible in the past because the risks are too high. Instruments on an unmanned cargo vessel measure oxygen, carbon dioxide, heat, pressure and flame growth, and two video cameras provide views of the flame. Results determine microgravity flammability limits for several spacecraft materials, help to validate NASA's material selection criteria, and how microgravity and limited oxygen affect flame size. Studying fire in small, sealed environments such as the Cygnus cargo supply vehicle benefits fire safety and prevention efforts on Earth, including inside mines, airplanes, or submarines.

title: Spacecraft Fire Experiment-II (SAFFIRE-II)
objectives: The objectives of SAFFIRE-II are to determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity and to investigate the low-g flammability limits compared to those obtained in NASA's normal gravity material flammability screening test.
approach: The Saffire-II experiment was performed on the Orbital Science's Cygnus resupply vehicle after it deberthed from the ISS. As a follow on to the Saffire-I investigation, the Saffire-II investigation added more samples including SIBAL, silicone, structure PMMA, flat PMMA, and PMMA with Nomex. The flight unit had a sample card installed in the middle of a large flow duct. Air is drawn through the flow duct by fans located at the top of the duct with flow straighteners at the bottom of the experiment module. Saffire-II has a sample card that contains 9 samples, each 5 cm x 29 cm. Depending on the sample material, Saffire-II was conducted at an air flow velocity of either 20 or 30 cm/s, the flow being either concurrent or opposed. Once the sample was ignited flame images were captured using two cameras. In addition, thermocouples provided flow, flame, and plume temperatures, two radiometers recorded flame radiation, solid state sensors were used to measure pressure, CO2 and O2 mole fraction, and two anemometers tracked flow velocity.
hypothesis: Same as SAFFIRE-I: large differences between fire behavior in normal and reduced gravity mean terrestrial fires and fire standards carry inherent uncertainty for spacecraft fire safety design; large-scale experiments in an expendable spacecraft fill the microgravity data gap without risk to a crew.
impacts: Same as SAFFIRE-I: realistic large-fire study on an exploration vehicle; microgravity flammability limits for several spacecraft materials; validation of NASA's material selection criteria; effect of microgravity and limited oxygen on flame size; Earth benefits for sealed environments (mines, airplanes, submarines).
key_results_from_table: Silicone samples (0.27, 0.61, 1.03 mm) at 20 cm/s concurrent and ~21.5-22.1% O2: microgravity burn length ~0 (did not sustain), whereas in 1-g the 0.27 mm sample burned completely with acceleratory spread and 0.61 mm burned 7.6 cm at 1.2 mm/s. SIBAL 0.37 mm concurrent at 20 cm/s: burned full 29 cm in microgravity at 2.1 mm/s (145 s burn).

title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME)
objectives: One of the major goals of this investigation was to quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulate achieves in low gravity and to relate the droplet size distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment. A numerical code was to be developed to predict the smoke droplet growth as a function of the fuel pyrolysis rate, the thermodynamic properties of the pyrolysis vapor, and the flow environment.
approach: The crew installed the near field hardware in the Glovebox, attached the Far Field Box to the Glovebox, and positioned the video cameras. The operator then ran the self diagnostic procedures on the two smoke detectors and activated the video cameras, turned on the igniter for a predefined period of time (15 to 60 seconds), and initiated the thermophoretic soot samplers to sample the smoke. The actual duration of each combustion event was typically 2 minutes. After flight, the particulate collected on the thermophoretic probes were analyzed using a Transmission Electron microscope (TEM) to determine primary and aggregate particle dimensions. The remains of the samples were weighed to determine their mass loss. The digital data was transcribed from the video record and analyzed to determine the response of the detectors. Once the flight mass loss rates were determined, 1-g operation conditions to produce the same loss were determined. The measurements were made using smoke generated by overheated spacecraft materials where variables such as the sample temperature, flow field, and particle aging time were more rigorously controlled.
hypothesis: In a μg environment, with the absence of the strong buoyancy-induced flows, smoke particle growth from a pyrolyzing/smoldering source, as a result of nucleation, condensation, and coagulation, will lead to larger particles compared to those produced in 1g. The formation of the larger particles is favored by the expected higher vapor concentration and smoke residence times near the source due to the reduced velocities and mixing at μg conditions. In particular, it is hypothesized that liquid aerosol smokes produced in microgravity will exhibit substantially larger droplet sizes than under the same conditions in normal gravity (with a corresponding decrease in the particle number density for the same mass of smoke). The change in the size distribution and number density will, in turn, affect the response of the smoke detectors and possibly result in some detectors not producing an alarm when exposed to this smoke.
impacts: The SAME experiment will provide technology for an advanced fire detector for future spacecraft that will be used for long duration missions. SAME will provide quantitative data on the sensitivity of these detectors to reduced gravity smokes that will allow evaluation of the adequacy of these existing technologies using relevant data. The current Fire Prevention, Detection, and Suppression (FPDS) program plan allows for the re-evaluation of future sensor technology. The results from SAME are needed to provide the reduced gravity baseline data against which future detection technology developments can be evaluated. The smoke detectors developed from the results of SAME can also be useful in other extreme environments on Earth, such as submarines or underwater laboratories.

title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight (SAME-R)
objectives: Similar to the original SAME investigation, the primary objective of the SAME-R investigation was to quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulate achieves in low gravity and to relate the droplet size distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment. One of the problems encountered during the SAME investigation was that after the thermal precipitators were returned to the ground, it was found that all the TEM grids were severely contaminated with some unidentified foreign particles, making these grids unusable although some of them showed shapes of certain types of smoke particles. Based on that experience the SAME-R investigation employed several modifications covering new materials, extended operating conditions, and diagnostic equipment.
approach: SAME-R utilized the SAME hardware used on-orbit. Based on the experience gained from SAME, SAME-R included the following modifications: 1) a new test material, Pyrell, an intumescent fire-retardant foam by Foamex, was introduced to replace DBP samples, 2) test conditions were broadened including higher heating temperatures and no-flow during sample heating time, and 3) a new instrument, M-pass, developed in-house at GRC, was used to replace one of the two Commercial Diagnostic Enclosures that includes a DustTrak and an ionization detector used in SAME. SAME-R flight tests were conducted from July 16 to September 9, 2010, successfully completing 66 test points. After SAME-R flight tests, three major post-flight ground tests were performed to improve data reduction process and to validate the lognormal distribution assumption, the key to the moment method employed by SAME and SAME-R.
hypothesis: Same hypotheses as SAME: in μg, without buoyancy-induced flows, smoke particles from pyrolyzing/smoldering sources grow larger (nucleation, condensation, coagulation) than in 1g, with lower number density for the same mass; this changes smoke detector response and may cause some detectors not to alarm.
impacts: Along with the results from the original SAME investigation, the results from SAME-R can lead to technology for an advanced fire detector for future spacecraft used for long duration missions; quantitative data on detector sensitivity to reduced-gravity smokes; baseline data for future detection technology under the Fire Prevention, Detection, and Suppression (FPDS) program; Earth applications in submarines or underwater laboratories.

title: Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX)
hardware: Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) - Fluids and Combustion Facility (FCF)

key_conditions.oxygen: varied down to non-ignition to find LOI

objectives: The FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) investigation aims to map the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity environments, measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6, and develop reliable predictive models for combustion limits under reduced gravity conditions. The mission seeks to validate and improve simplified models by incorporating detailed chemical reactions, heat transfer, and material movement, using both space-based data and extensive ground-based tests. Key flight experiment goals include obtaining high-resolution measurements of droplet burning rates, flame extinction behavior, heat radiation, soot levels, and temperature profiles, while systematically analyzing the effects of different ambient conditions and suppressant concentrations.
approach: The FLEX experiments involve igniting and observing the burning behavior of relatively large droplets. A primary objective of the experiments is to determine the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) as a function of ambient pressure and determine how the presence of a suppressant influences the LOI. Procedure: 1. Select the test pressure (0.5 − 1.5 atm) for the LOI tests. 2. Select a smaller droplet size (≈ 3 mm). 3. Select an ambient oxygen mole fraction that, based on ground-based testing, will support droplets burning to completion. 4. Perform a droplet combustion test. 5. Increase the droplet size or repeat the test (if finite extinction diameter at flame extinction observed). 6. Continue steps 4 and 5 until flame exists for only a short time after ignition (radiative extinction). 7. Continue steps 4 thru 6 at a decreased ambient oxygen mole fraction. 8. Continue step 7 to an ambient oxygen mole fraction where the droplet does not ignite. Where extinction droplet sizes were too small to observe, the LOI was found iteratively (burn to completion followed by a no-ignition test) with progressively smaller increments in oxygen mole fraction. In slow-flow tests, near the end of burning the droplet is subjected to a small, sub-buoyant convective flow (by translating the droplet at a slow uniform speed) to see how this flow influences extinction. Many tests involve free (unsupported) droplets, some with a slow drift velocity.
hypothesis: The primary hypothesis of the FLEX mission is that microgravity conditions fundamentally alter the combustion and extinction characteristics of liquid fuel droplets due to changes in species and energy transport dynamics, radiative heat loss, and chemical kinetics. Specifically, the lack of buoyant convection in microgravity will lead to significant differences in the flammability limits and suppression efficacy of various fire suppressant agents compared to normal gravity conditions.
impacts: Improved fire safety protocols for future space missions where traditional fire suppression methods may be ineffective. On Earth, insights can advance fire safety in confined and reduced-gravity environments, such as submarines or high-altitude aircraft. Findings on the effectiveness of suppressants (CO2, He, SF6) in microgravity can lead to more efficient and less harmful fire suppression systems, reducing the risk of toxic byproducts. The study of 'cool flames' and low-temperature combustion observed in microgravity can inform the design of advanced combustion engines with improved fuel efficiency and reduced emissions.
notable_discovery: FLEX revealed quasi-steady droplet burning supported by 'cool flames' (low-temperature chemistry) after radiative extinction of the hot flame for n-alkanes (see Nayagam et al., 'Can cool flames support quasi-steady alkane droplet burning?' 2012).

title: Flame Extinguishment Experiment - 2 (FLEX-2)
proposal_title: The Fundamental Studies in Droplet Combustion and Flame Extinguishment in Microgravity

variables: droplet spacing and initial size in a binary linear array

objectives: The primary goal of the FLEX-2 flight experiments is to extend the results of FLEX-1 to fuels and environmental conditions that mimic real combustor conditions, as well as provide benchmark experimental data on bi-component droplet combustion over a wide range of initial conditions in order to validate numerical simulations and to develop new theoretical models. Detailed objectives: 1. Investigate the role of liquid-phase mixing on the burning characteristics of bi-component fuel droplets. 2. Examine the steady and unsteady liquid and gas-phase phenomena in pure fuel combustion. 3. Study flame extinction mechanisms and their boundaries. 4. Analyze the soot formation process, including soot volume fraction and soot-shell dynamics. 5. Determine the influence of droplet interactions on the flammability limits and extinction behavior of droplet arrays. 6. Validate theoretical models of droplet combustion through comprehensive experimental data collection in microgravity environments.
approach: The chamber was filled with the appropriate atmosphere, varied in pressure between 0.5 atm and 3.0 atm and O2 concentration between 0.1 and 0.4 mole fraction with the diluent gas making up the balance. A settling time of approximately 2 minutes ensured stable temperature and pressure. A predetermined amount of fuel (based on target droplet size) was dispensed onto the support fiber for tests where the droplet is not freely deployed; after needle retraction, a dwell of at least 10 seconds let internal fluid motion subside. The ignitor was powered for 1 to 5 seconds then retracted. If the flow field was generated by translating the droplet, motion began when the ignitor retracted. Near real-time color video verified deployment, ignition and progress; chamber pressure and temperature were recorded. Steps: determine test parameters (pressure, temperature, fuel mixture, humidity); fill chamber; deploy droplet(s) controlling diameter; stabilize; ignite; track flame evolution with high-speed photography; adjust; analyze data.
hypothesis: Sophisticated numerical simulations of convective droplet combustion now include full Navier-Stokes gas-phase flow, but use approximations for chemistry, radiation, and gas-liquid coupling whose validity has not been confirmed with benchmark data. In microgravity, buoyancy is minimized, and the droplet can be characterized only as a function of thermocapillary or solutal-capillary stresses, allowing clear observation of fundamental processes, including transitions between radiative and diffusive extinction of the flame. The goal is benchmark data on bi-component droplet combustion to validate simulations and develop new theoretical models.
impacts: Liquid fuel combustion is the overwhelming energy source in transportation. Benefits: more sustainable energy production; combustor designs with minimal carbon footprint, maximum fuel efficiency and fewer pollutant emissions; quantitative evaluation of future fuels through surrogates (mixtures of pure fuels that simulate real fuels); validation of jet engine models by engine manufacturers.
